defects.description: The download links are presigned with the Fargate task role's temporary credentials. They are emailed at about 02:25 and will probably expire before managers open them in the morning. The design states this correctly and offers an API Gateway + Lambda re-sign endpoint as an open question, but it does not adopt that fix, so R4 (a usable emailed download link) is not reliably met.
defects.evidence: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html ("If you created a presigned URL using a temporary credential, the URL expires when the credential expires"; "For Amazon Elastic Container Service tasks or containers, role credentials typically rotate every 1-6 hours.")

defects.description: The Scheduler DLQ only catches failures to start the task. A task that starts and then exits non-zero is not covered: no EventBridge rule on ECS Task State Change and no metric filter is modelled, even though CloudWatch claims to alarm on failed runs.

The task runs in a public subnet with a public IP so it can skip NAT. This is acceptable with no inbound rules, but the internet-reachable ENI should be acknowledged as a trade-off. The S3 bucket policy should also deny non-TLS access.

reviews.summary: A lean, correct Scheduler -> Fargate -> S3/SES design with good alerting, but the emailed presigned links will likely expire before managers use them, and that fix is left as an open question.

defects.description: Like A, the links are presigned with task-role temporary credentials, which expire within hours. The design acknowledges this but provides no working alternative, so managers reading email in the morning will probably get expired links.
defects.evidence: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html ("For Amazon Elastic Container Service tasks or containers, role credentials typically rotate every 1-6 hours.")

defects.description: R8 (a failed or missed run is detected and alerted) has no delivery path. There is a CloudWatch alarm but no SNS topic or recipient, no DLQ or retry policy on the schedule target, and no ECS task-state event rule. A missed run would go unnoticed.

A NAT Gateway, billed hourly plus per-GB processed, is added only for egress. For a ~25-minute nightly job under a 'cheap' constraint it will likely be the largest line item. Gateway endpoints or a public-IP task would be cheaper.
ECR (the image source) is not modelled. The rationale also contains a leaked tool-internal reference ('fixes VR-009').

reviews.summary: Functionally similar to A, but it pays for a NAT Gateway, omits the image registry, and its failure alerting has no notification target.

defects.description: Alerts are published to a single SNS 'Alert topic'. Publishing to a topic delivers to every subscribed phone number, so with SMS subscriptions all owners would get every device's alerts. The design has no owner/phone/threshold registry for targeting each owner's number with a direct Publish to PhoneNumber.
defects.evidence: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_sending-overview.html ("When you publish a message to a topic, Amazon SNS attempts to deliver that message to every phone number that is subscribed to the topic.")

defects.description: R5 claims owners can view only their own device data, but there is no device-to-owner mapping. The query Lambda reads by deviceId without any ownership check, so any authenticated user could query any device (an IDOR flaw).

There is no alert deduplication or cooldown. A device that stays out of range would send an SMS every minute; the deviceId+timestamp dedupe key does not prevent this. This hurts both cost and user experience.

Every reading (~833/s, ~2.16B/month) goes through Lambda before reaching DynamoDB. The IoT rule DynamoDBv2 action could write directly, with only alert evaluation in Lambda. No IoT rule error action is configured.

reviews.summary: A sound serverless IoT Core/DynamoDB/Cognito skeleton, but SMS targeting via a shared topic, missing owner-to-device authorization and missing alert dedupe are significant gaps.

defects.description: The alert Lambda is invoked asynchronously for every reading (~2.16B invocations/month). An IoT rule WHERE pre-filter, or batching, could cut this substantially.

Downsampling 90 days of per-minute data (~129,600 items) on every dashboard read is costly in DynamoDB RCUs and latency. Pre-aggregated rollups would be better; the design raises this only as an open question.
No IoT rule error action is modelled for DynamoDBv2 or Lambda action failures, so failed rule actions surface only as metrics.

reviews.summary: A production-grade MVP: per-device topic-scoped IoT policies, direct rule-to-DynamoDB writes with TTL, a registry for ownership and SMS targeting, deduplicated alerts and a DLQ.

defects.description: The failure destination is described as configured 'on the S3 ObjectCreated edge'. S3 notifications have no failure destination; it is part of the Lambda asynchronous invocation config. The edge from ingest-fn reading the PDF from the bucket is also missing.

Loading the initial 20,000 PDFs triggers Lambda directly with no buffering or concurrency control, so Bedrock embedding throttling during bulk load would exhaust async retries and flood the failure queue.
HTTP API integrations time out at 30 seconds. RAG retrieval plus LLM generation can approach this, and neither streaming nor the timeout is addressed.
Per-customer history isolation and the OpenSearch access policy are not specified. Customer-managed KMS keys add cost and key management with no stated requirement.

reviews.summary: A correct basic Bedrock + OpenSearch RAG design with Cognito-gated chat and TTL history, but ingestion is unbuffered and a few configuration details are imprecise.

defects.description: HTTP API integrations time out at 30 seconds. Streaming is raised as an open question, but the hard timeout risk for non-streamed LLM answers is not stated.
A provisioned OpenSearch domain has a fixed baseline cost. Sizing and the choice of domain vs serverless collection are not discussed.

reviews.summary: A well-built RAG pipeline: S3 -> SQS -> Lambda with partial batch responses, a DLQ and idempotent chunk IDs, plus per-user history keyed by Cognito sub and explicit citation metadata.

preference.why: A avoids the NAT Gateway cost, models ECR, and has a complete alerting path (Scheduler DLQ -> CloudWatch -> SNS -> ops), while both share the presigned-link expiry gap.
B has a device registry for ownership checks and per-owner SMS, deduplicated alerts and direct rule-to-DynamoDB writes, where A has none of these.
B buffers ingestion through SQS with a DLQ and idempotent upserts, and it explicitly isolates history per customer and defines citation metadata.
